Monday, November 9, 2026 Daily Digest

OpenAI Claims ChatGPT Search Hits 20% of Google's Volume — But Drives Only 0.36% of Referral Traffic, Perplexity Launches "Teammates" AI Agents

Today's top stories in AI + enterprise tech

1

OpenAI: ChatGPT Search Volume Is Now 20% of Google's — But Ahrefs Data Shows It Drives Just 0.36% of Website Traffic

At an OpenAI dinner in New York on November 2, ChatGPT consumer product lead Adam Fry told Big Technology's Alex Kantrowitz that "ChatGPT's volume of search-like queries is now roughly one-fifth the volume of queries of Google." Fry also revealed that ChatGPT has grown from 1 billion to 1.2 billion weekly active users in just two months — roughly 100 million new users every 30 days. But the impressive query volume figure obscures a critical gap: according to Ahrefs data covering 118,671 websites, Google sent 24.74% of all tracked referral traffic in October while ChatGPT sent just 0.36%. The two measures are not in conflict — one counts questions asked inside ChatGPT, the other counts visits that leave it. Most ChatGPT answers never send anyone anywhere. For marketers and B2B teams, this creates a measurement blind spot: buyers are asking AI more questions, but far fewer of those questions result in clicks your analytics can see. A buyer can read a summary that names your company, shortlist you, and arrive weeks later as a direct visit or branded Google search, with nothing in your reports connecting the dots. OpenAI also announced plans to merge ChatGPT's Chat and Work modes and put both on a shared usage allowance starting in December.

Perplexity Launches "Teammates" — AI Agents That Own Ongoing Responsibilities Across Marketing, Sales, and Operations

Perplexity announced "Teammates" on November 4, a new category of AI agents designed to manage complex, ongoing projects rather than answering single prompts. Unlike traditional AI assistants that respond to individual queries, Teammates are built to own continuing responsibilities — tracking competitors, monitoring market trends, managing research workflows, or handling recurring operational tasks. The feature launched for Perplexity Max subscribers at $200/month. Engadget reports that Teammates coordinate multiple AI agents, manage projects across business functions including marketing, sales, customer support, operations, and finance, and follow through without requiring constant human prompting. The positioning marks a significant shift from AI as question-answerer to AI as persistent worker. For enterprise teams, this raises the familiar challenge of measurement and governance: when an AI agent is responsible for ongoing work rather than discrete tasks, how do you audit what it's doing, verify its outputs, and ensure it stays aligned with business objectives? Perplexity is betting that the "single agent per session" model is giving way to persistent agents that act more like employees than tools — a bet that will require new frameworks for accountability.

Trump Tells 60 Minutes He "Doesn't Mind Guardrails" on AI — But Frames the Issue Entirely as a Race with China

In his first post-midterm 60 Minutes interview, President Trump told Ross Douthat that AI risks "can be managed," named DOJ as the manager, and said "I don't mind guardrails" — as long as the US is not pushed into "a deep second position" to China. Trump invoked China eight times in the exchange, framing AI regulation almost entirely as a competitive race rather than a safety problem. He signaled openness to working with Democrats on safeguards but would not specify which guardrails he would sign. The interview comes days after Democrats swept the midterms with campaigns that challenged big tech, and tech stocks plunged 5.5% on fears of tighter AI regulation. For enterprise AI buyers, the political signal is mixed: the administration appears open to some form of AI governance, but only insofar as it doesn't slow the competitive race with China. That framing may complicate efforts to establish clear, predictable rules for AI deployment. The emphasis on DOJ as the regulatory body — rather than a dedicated AI safety office — suggests enforcement-focused governance rather than proactive standard-setting.

Cognition CISO Alex Stamos: AI Has Pushed Cybersecurity Into a Multi-Year "Dark Age" — Defenses Can't Keep Up

In a Decoder interview with Nilay Patel, newly announced Cognition CISO Alex Stamos — former Facebook and Yahoo CSO — warned that open-weight AI models now automate most of the cyber kill chain and have inverted it. Bug finding and exploit writing now happen live, per target, rather than being stockpiled, he said. Both private and state-aligned actors from Russia and North Korea are using AI to discover and exploit vulnerabilities simultaneously. Stamos predicted the multibillion-dollar cyber industry "will be buckling for several years before defenses catch up." The warning follows last week's reports of GPT-6 Cyber finding 948 Linux kernel exploits and Claude discovering Xen CVEs. For enterprise security teams, the implication is that the traditional model of patching known vulnerabilities is increasingly inadequate — adversaries can now find new vulnerabilities faster than defenders can patch them. Stamos's framing suggests that organizations need to assume breach and focus on detection and response rather than prevention alone. The "dark age" framing isn't hyperbole when AI-discovered zero-days become routine.

US Professional Services Add 70K Jobs in October — Largest Monthly Gain Since July 2022, Despite AI Displacement Fears

US professional and business services added 70,000 jobs in October, the largest monthly gain since July 2022, according to Wall Street Journal analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Consulting added 17,300 jobs, legal services added 2,400, and accounting added 2,300 — all sectors frequently cited as highly exposed to AI displacement. The data complicates the narrative that AI is rapidly eliminating white-collar work. However, the picture is nuanced: narrower roles within these categories are showing pressure, with document processing and routine analysis tasks being automated even as higher-judgment work expands. The job gains may reflect several factors: enterprises need more consultants to help them implement AI, legal and accounting work is growing in complexity as AI creates new regulatory questions, and the labor market lag means displacement effects may not yet be visible in aggregate data. For enterprise leaders, the October numbers suggest that AI is reshaping professional services more than shrinking them — at least for now. The question is whether this pattern holds as AI capabilities continue to advance.

📊 My Take

The 20% vs 0.36% gap is the marketing measurement story of 2026. When OpenAI says ChatGPT handles a fifth as many search-like queries as Google but Ahrefs shows it drives barely a third of a percent of referral traffic, you're looking at a new kind of invisible influence. Buyers are researching in AI, but they're not clicking through. They're arriving later, via direct visits or branded searches, with no attribution trail connecting the dots.

This is why the "just optimize for AI search" advice is incomplete. Yes, you need to show up in AI answers — but your analytics will dramatically undercount the impact. The teams who figure out how to track this influence (asking "how did you hear about us?" with an AI option, running branded queries through ChatGPT monthly, logging what sales hears on calls) will have a massive advantage over those who keep staring at referral dashboards that show essentially nothing.

Perplexity's Teammates launch is the next evolution: from AI that answers questions to AI that owns ongoing work. The shift from prompt-response to persistent agent is the shift from tool to employee — and it brings all the governance challenges of hiring someone who works 24/7 with perfect memory and no natural breaks for reflection. The measurement frameworks that barely work for one-shot AI tasks won't survive the move to continuous operation.

And Stamos's "dark age" warning connects to everything else. If AI-powered adversaries can find vulnerabilities faster than defenders can patch them, the entire assumption that you can secure systems by staying current collapses. The enterprises spending 2.5x over budget on AI while only 13% see significant value need to be asking whether their security posture is keeping pace with their deployment ambitions. Based on Stamos's assessment, it probably isn't.
